question: From the beginning, the church faced trouble from those who taught false doctrine about Jesus Christ. Even today, people still lead others astray by false teachings about Jesus Christ. Explain these two false teachings about the personhood of Jesus Christ: (a) Arianism (b) Docetism.
idealAnswer: Heresies have arisen in Christian history whenever either Christ’s deity or his humanity has been neglected, and from the very beginning the Church faced trouble from those who taught false doctrines about Jesus. Two such false teachings are Arianism and Docetism. Arianism is the first false idea, that Jesus was just a man and not God at all. It is the denial of Christ’s divinity and takes its name from Arius of Alexandria, who died in 335. Arius taught that the Son of God and the Holy Spirit were beings willed into existence by God for the purposes of redemption; they were therefore not eternal as God is, and there was a time “before which they were not.” Those who hold this view are willing to agree that Jesus was a great moral teacher whom God blessed, but they deny that Jesus was God. Docetism is exactly the opposite error: that Jesus was God but not man. It is the denial of Christ’s humanity, and the name comes from the Greek verb dokeo, which means “to appear” or “to seem.” Docetism asserts very strongly that Jesus was divine but denies that he really was human; he only seemed to be a man, and his human nature was only a mask behind which his true divine self was concealed. On this view Jesus was not a real man but a spiritual being who looked like a man, acted like a man and seemed to be a man, but was not really subject to the limitations and problems of earthly human existence. In him God was only pretending to be with us in the midst of our sinful, suffering, creaturely existence, and his purpose was not to help us in the world but to help us escape from it.

topic: The Biblical Source of the Doctrine of the Trinity
question: We cannot find the doctrine of the Trinity spelt out in the scriptures. However, we can find that there are roots of the doctrine in the scriptures. Trace the roots of the doctrine of the Trinity in the New Testament.
idealAnswer: The Bible nowhere teaches the doctrine of the Trinity in so many words – neither the word “trinity” nor the language of “one-in-three”, “essence” or “persons” is biblical language – but the roots of the doctrine are clearly there. In the New Testament, according to Robert Culver, two expressions have traditionally been used to designate the inner relations of the Father, the Son and the Spirit: the eternal generation of the Son by the Father, and the eternal aspiration or procession of the Spirit from the Father and the Son. In scriptural language these express the idea that the Son and the Spirit were eternal with the Godhead: John 1:14 refers to our Lord as the only begotten Son of the Father, and John 14:16, 26 speak of the Spirit as proceeding from the Father. The preaching of John the Baptist, as R. A. Finlayson suggests, most probably had a Trinitarian reference, since he was conscious of the presence and calling of the Spirit. At the baptism of Jesus in the Jordan the three persons can be distinguished: the Son being baptized, the Father speaking from heaven, and the Spirit descending in the objective symbol of a dove. In his public ministry and in his private teaching of the Twelve, Jesus constantly directed attention to the Father as the one who sent him and from whom he derived his authority, and he bore clear testimony to the Father and to the Spirit in the work of redemption – the Father sending the Son to undertake the work, and the Father and the Son sending the Spirit to apply the salvation. The most concise expression of Trinitarian teaching by Christ is the baptismal formula, “baptizing into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). The Pentecost experience shows the apostolic conception of the Spirit and of his relation to the Father and the Son, for Peter explains the event as the activity of the Triune God; and the apostolic benediction shows that the apostolic church was built upon faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, redemption being uniformly traced in the epistles to this threefold source.
keyPoints: The doctrine itself is not spelt out in Scripture, but its roots are found there
Culver’s two expressions: the eternal generation of the Son by the Father, and the eternal procession of the Spirit
John 1:14 – the only begotten Son of the Father; John 14:16, 26 – the Spirit proceeding from the Father
John the Baptist’s preaching had a Trinitarian reference
Jesus’ baptism – the Son baptized, the Father speaking from heaven, the Spirit descending as a dove
Jesus’ public ministry – he points to the Father who sent him and to the Spirit in the work of redemption

The Pentecost experience and the apostolic benediction

question: Write short notes on five facts about the resurrection of Jesus Christ that Christians need to bear in mind.
idealAnswer: The resurrection is the central doctrine of Christianity, affirming that God raised Jesus from the dead on the third day; without it, Paul declared, Christian preaching and belief are meaningless, there would be no church and we would still be in our sins. Five things Christians need to know about it are these. First, it is the foundation of the Christian faith: it lifts Christianity from the level of philosophy or a mere code of conduct to the stature of God’s good news for the human race, for in the resurrection God set his seal of approval upon Christ as Son of God and underlined the value of his death; it transformed the followers of Jesus and sent them out to preach, and it is the non-negotiable pivot of the faith. Second, it is an event supported by evidence: there is factual evidence – the empty tomb with only the abandoned grave clothes, the failure of every other explanation, and the numerous reported appearances of the risen Jesus at different times and before different people – and psychological evidence – the transformed disciples, the conviction of the early church under persecution, and the change of the day of worship from Saturday to Sunday. Third, it is a promise of ultimate victory: had Christ not been raised, his death would have been evidence enough of the failure of his mission, but the resurrection assures the believer that he has not believed in vain and that all things, even the last enemy, death, must submit to the victory and rule of Jesus. Fourth, it is the power of Christian experience: the resurrection is far more than a past event, for it plays a vital part in Christian living now and colours the outlook, hopes and motives of every believer, who lives and works in the very power by which God raised Jesus from the dead. Fifth, it is the assurance of eternal security: the finality has been taken out of death, for all who die know that Christ has been through the experience before them and will bring them through it to be with him, and because Christ’s body was raised the Christian is guaranteed a resurrection body of beauty and strength, related to the old but without weakness or decay.

God set his seal of approval upon Christ as Son of God and underlined the value of his death

question: From the beginning, the church faced trouble from those who taught false doctrine about Jesus Christ. Even today, people still lead others astray by false teachings about Jesus Christ. Explain these two false teachings about the personhood of Jesus Christ: (a) Arianism (b) Docetism.
idealAnswer: Heresies have arisen in Christian history whenever either Christ’s deity or his humanity has been neglected, and from the very beginning the Church faced trouble from those who taught false doctrines about Jesus. Two such false teachings are Arianism and Docetism. Arianism is the first false idea, that Jesus was just a man and not God at all. It is the denial of Christ’s divinity and takes its name from Arius of Alexandria, who died in 335. Arius taught that the Son of God and the Holy Spirit were beings willed into existence by God for the purposes of redemption; they were therefore not eternal as God is, and there was a time “before which they were not.” Those who hold this view are willing to agree that Jesus was a great moral teacher whom God blessed, but they deny that Jesus was God. Docetism is exactly the opposite error: that Jesus was God but not man. It is the denial of Christ’s humanity, and the name comes from the Greek verb dokeo, which means “to appear” or “to seem.” Docetism asserts very strongly that Jesus was divine but denies that he really was human; he only seemed to be a man, and his human nature was only a mask behind which his true divine self was concealed. On this view Jesus was not a real man but a spiritual being who looked like a man, acted like a man and seemed to be a man, but was not really subject to the limitations and problems of earthly human existence. In him God was only pretending to be with us in the midst of our sinful, suffering, creaturely existence, and his purpose was not to help us in the world but to help us escape from it.

subject: DOC
topic: The Biblical Source of the Doctrine of the Trinity
question: We cannot find the terminology “Trinity” spelled out in the scriptures. However, we can find that there are roots of the doctrine in the scriptures. Trace the roots of the doctrine of the Trinity in both the New and the Old Testaments.
idealAnswer: The Bible does not teach the doctrine of the Trinity as such: neither the word “trinity” itself nor language such as “one-in-three”, “three-in-one”, one “essence” or “substance”, or three “persons” is biblical language. While the doctrine itself is not spelt out in Scripture, its roots are clearly there. In the Old Testament the first root is the creation story, where Elohim is seen to create by means of Word and Spirit (Gen. 1:1-3), revealing a threefold centre of activity in which God the creator thought out the universe, expressed his thought in a Word, and made his Spirit its animating principle; and the name Elohim in Genesis 1:1 is itself plural in form though joined to a singular verb. A second root is the creation of man and the use of personal pronouns in the plural form, for in Genesis 1:26 God says, “Let us make man in our image and after our likeness,” which by implication reveals God as the Triune God. A third root is the threefold Aaronic blessing of Numbers 6:24, which is a prototype of the New Testament apostolic blessing. In the New Testament, Robert Culver notes two traditional expressions for the inner relations of the persons: the eternal generation of the Son by the Father and the eternal procession of the Spirit from the Father and the Son; John 1:14 speaks of the only begotten Son of the Father and John 14:16, 26 of the Spirit as proceeding from the Father. The preaching of John the Baptist most probably had a Trinitarian reference. At the baptism of Jesus in the Jordan the three persons can be distinguished: the Son being baptized, the Father speaking from heaven and the Spirit descending as a dove. In his public ministry Jesus constantly directed attention to the Father who sent him, and testified to the Father and the Spirit in the work of redemption. The most concise expression of Trinitarian teaching by Christ is the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19. Finally, Peter explains the Pentecost experience as the activity of the Triune God, and the apostolic benediction shows that the apostolic church was built upon faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
keyPoints: The doctrine is not spelt out in Scripture, but its roots are found there
Old Testament: creation – Elohim creates by Word and Spirit (Gen. 1:1-3)
Elohim is plural in form but joined to a singular verb
Genesis 1:26 – “let us make man in our image” uses plural pronouns
The threefold Aaronic blessing of Numbers 6:24
New Testament: eternal generation of the Son and procession of the Spirit
John the Baptist’s preaching, Jesus’ baptism and public ministry
The baptismal formula (Matt. 28:19), Pentecost and the apostolic benediction

subject: DOC
topic: History of the Formulation of the Nicene Creed
question: Briefly trace the history of the formulation of the Nicene Creed.
idealAnswer: The whole issue of the formulation of the creed began with questions about the person of Christ: “Who was he?” “Was he God or Man?” By the beginning of the fourth century the answer to this question was not clear. One of those who attempted an answer was Arius, a presbyter from Alexandria, who said that the Son, Jesus Christ, was a creature and not God. For him only God the Father is unbegotten and self-subsistent; the Son is begotten, so there must have been a time when he was not. His main reason was that there is only one God, so that if the Son is also God we should have two Gods. This view was strongly opposed by Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, who suspended Arius from office; but Arius stuck to his opinions and received support from friends and sympathizers, so that the dispute spread and became a threat to the unity of the church as well as of the empire. Consequently Emperor Constantine summoned the first great ecumenical council of Bishops to meet at Nicaea in 325. The council condemned Arianism and drafted a creed to which all the bishops were required to assent. That creed was not the one we now call the Nicene Creed, but it attempted the very difficult task of saying affirmatively what the essentials of Christian belief are in a way that excluded any possible Arian interpretation; its most noteworthy feature was the assertion that Christ is “of one substance as the Father”. Peace did not follow quickly. In 328 Athanasius became bishop of Alexandria; already in his treatise De Incarnatione, usually dated 318, he had contributed a “Christology of the Word, which took a body of the virgin”, arguing that only God, the Uncreated, can save us and give us life, so that a creature, even the highest, cannot. The views of Athanasius and his supporters finally triumphed only some years after his death, at an ecumenical council held at Constantinople in 381. It was this council which agreed to what we now call the Nicene Creed, though it would be more accurately called the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed, and it enshrined the word homoousios, “of the same being” or “consubstantial”, as the most accurate term the church could find to express the relation of Christ to the Father. That same council also discussed the divinity of the Holy Spirit, which had been denied at Nicaea, and officially accepted and affirmed it. The creed of 381 remains to this day the most ecumenical of all dogmatic statements in the Christian churches.

subject: DOC
question: Write short notes on five facts about the resurrection of Jesus Christ that Christians need to bear in mind.
idealAnswer: The resurrection is the central doctrine of Christianity, affirming that God raised Jesus from the dead on the third day; without it, Paul declared, Christian preaching and belief are meaningless, there would be no church and we would still be in our sins. Five things Christians need to know about it are these. First, it is the foundation of the Christian faith: it lifts Christianity from the level of philosophy or a mere code of conduct to the stature of God’s good news for the human race, for in the resurrection God set his seal of approval upon Christ as Son of God and underlined the value of his death; it transformed the followers of Jesus and sent them out to preach, and it is the non-negotiable pivot of the faith. Second, it is an event supported by evidence: there is factual evidence – the empty tomb with only the abandoned grave clothes, the failure of every other explanation, and the numerous reported appearances of the risen Jesus at different times and before different people – and psychological evidence – the transformed disciples, the conviction of the early church under persecution, and the change of the day of worship from Saturday to Sunday. Third, it is a promise of ultimate victory: had Christ not been raised, his death would have been evidence enough of the failure of his mission, but the resurrection assures the believer that he has not believed in vain and that all things, even the last enemy, death, must submit to the victory and rule of Jesus. Fourth, it is the power of Christian experience: the resurrection is far more than a past event, for it plays a vital part in Christian living now and colours the outlook, hopes and motives of every believer, who lives and works in the very power by which God raised Jesus from the dead. Fifth, it is the assurance of eternal security: the finality has been taken out of death, for all who die know that Christ has been through the experience before them and will bring them through it to be with him, and because Christ’s body was raised the Christian is guaranteed a resurrection body of beauty and strength, related to the old but without weakness or decay.

God set his seal of approval upon Christ as Son of God
It is an event supported by evidence – the empty tomb, grave clothes, appearances
Psychological evidence – transformed disciples, the persecuted church, Saturday changed to Sunday
It is a promise of ultimate victory – death, the last enemy, must submit to Jesus
It is the power of Christian experience
It is the assurance of eternal security – the finality is taken out of death
The Christian is guaranteed a resurrection body without weakness or decay

subject: DOC
chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
topic: Hallmark of the Gifts of the Spirit
question: What will you tell your congregation, in a teaching service, about the differences between the fruit of the Spirit and the gifts of the Spirit?
idealAnswer: The fruit of the Spirit and the gifts of the Spirit are both the work of the one Holy Spirit, but they differ. The fruit of the Spirit is concerned with character, while the gifts of the Spirit relate to abilities and functions distributed among believers. All the fruit should be exhibited in every Christian, but the gifts differ widely from person to person. The fruit is singular, not plural: Paul writes in Galatians 5:22-23 that “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control,” so there are not nine fruits but one fruit composed of nine elements, and the one kind of fruit the Spirit produces is Christ-likeness. Unlike the gifts, only some of which are given to a Christian, each believer is to have all nine virtues composing the fruit; and as fruit on a tree takes time to grow and mature, so the Spirit does not cultivate these virtues in a believer’s life overnight. The fruit is not produced by human effort but as Christians live in communion with the Lord, and it is the evidence of salvation and of the genuine work of the Spirit. The gifts, by contrast, began to be given when the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples at Pentecost and will continue until Christ comes again. They are not restricted to outstanding individuals or leaders: each believer has at least one gift, no one believer possesses all the gifts, and so the members of the Church need one another. Their hallmarks are that they glorify Christ, they involve all, they should unite all, they lay foundations, they edify the Church and they promote its mission; and they can be abused – by not using them in love, by neglecting the gifts imparted to us, or by attempting to use gifts not imparted to us.
keyPoints: The fruit is concerned with character; the gifts relate to abilities and functions
All the fruit should be exhibited in every Christian; the gifts differ widely from person to person
The fruit is singular – one fruit of nine elements (Gal. 5:22-23) – and its kind is Christ-likeness
The fruit takes time to mature and is not produced by human effort
The gifts began at Pentecost and continue until Christ comes again
Each believer has at least one gift; no believer has all the gifts
Hallmarks of the gifts: they glorify Christ, involve all, unite all, lay foundations, edify the Church, promote mission
The gifts can be abused

chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE LAST THINGS (ESCHATOLOGY)
question: Write an essay on any two (2) of the elements of the Last Things (Eschatology).
idealAnswer: Christians are not in full agreement about the details of the future events; they disagree about the millennium and about the great tribulation. But regardless of those disagreements most writers focus on the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body and the final judgment as the essential and dominant elements of eschatology. Take first the return of Christ. Most of the Old Testament prophecies about the coming of Christ deal not with his first advent, in which he died as our sin-bearer, but with his Second Advent, in which he is to rule as king; in the New Testament one verse in twenty-five deals with the Lord’s return, and it is mentioned in every New Testament book except Galatians and the very short books. Paul called it “our blessed hope” and Peter our “living hope”. It is a practical doctrine, not merely an escape route for wishful thoughts: the early Christians associated it with a period of great wickedness on earth, the resurrection and transformation of their bodies, an earthly rule of the glorified Jesus and a final judgment of individuals and nations, and they acknowledged that their lives should be lived differently because of it. It comforts those who suffer and those who have been bereaved, and it is an encouragement to godly living. Take second the resurrection of the body – specifically the resurrection of the bodies of believers at Christ’s Second Coming. This doctrine recognizes that death is an enemy, something unnatural and evil that was not God’s original intention for humanity, against the false optimism which denies the reality of sin, suffering and death; and it speaks of the victory over death provided for us by the Lord Jesus. Death involves every part of our being, for Adam and Eve died in spirit, soul and body; and when God saves us he saves us in spirit, soul and body – a new spirit at the new birth, a new soul through sanctification, and a new body at the resurrection – so that the salvation he provides is a complete salvation. Our assurance of these things rests upon Christ’s own resurrection. The third element, the Day of Judgement, means that history has an end and that its end involves accountability: Christ will come to judge the living and the dead, and we shall be judged either on the basis of our own righteousness, which will condemn us, or on the basis of the perfect righteousness of Jesus our Saviour, as Jesus taught in the parables of the Ten Virgins, the Talents, and the Sheep and Goats.
keyPoints: The essential and dominant elements are the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body and the final judgment
Christians disagree about the millennium and the great tribulation
Christ’s return is mentioned in every New Testament book except Galatians and the very short books
Paul called it “our blessed hope”; Peter called it our “living hope”
The return is a practical doctrine – it shapes conduct, comforts sufferers and the bereaved, and encourages godly living
The resurrection of the body recognizes death as an enemy and proclaims victory over it
God saves us in spirit, soul and body – a complete salvation, assured by Christ’s own resurrection
The Day of Judgement means history has an end and that end involves accountability

topic: The Relevance of the Doctrine of the Trinity
question: Discuss the relevance of the doctrine of the Trinity.
idealAnswer: The doctrine of the Trinity is ultimately a practical doctrine with radical consequences for Christian experience and life. First, it shapes relationships. According to the doctrine, God lives as the mystery of love among persons; since we are created in the image and likeness of this God and our destiny is to live for ever with him and with his beloved creatures, the doctrine of the Trinity is a way of contemplating the mystery of God and of ourselves in relation to God, and the framework for reflecting on the nature of the human person and on our relationship with the other creatures of the earth. Christians are baptized into the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and since names express personal identity, to live in the name of another is to appropriate their personal history. Secondly, it shapes our relationship with others. The Godhead reveals that God is truly a living one, not impersonal but personal, who relates and deals with us at one and the same time as loving Father, self-giving Saviour and sanctifying Spirit. The Triune God is Love and is always in love: St. Augustine said that without the Trinity there can be no fellowship as love in God. The Trinity teaches that God is indivisibly one, with unity of purpose and action, the three persons living and working harmoniously together for the final realization of the Kingdom of God, so that as we worship the God of unity we too are called to unity. The Trinity also brings to the fore the communal nature of God: the three persons live in mutual co-existence, solidarity, fellowship and harmony, with no power struggle or personality conflict, and those who embrace this are under a moral and spiritual obligation to promote fellowship, solidarity and harmonious communal existence, and through this freedom, justice, peace and prosperity. Thirdly, the doctrine shapes prayer. St. Augustine acknowledged the active presence and involvement of the Triune God in the prayer of Christians, each Person playing his distinct role: we pray to the Father with the assurance that it is God himself who has given us the power to become children of God; prayers are addressed to Christ, as well as through him and in his name, for Jesus taught his disciples to pray and set the example by praying himself; and in prayer the Holy Spirit is the Christian’s master who animates the prayer and enables us to discover God as our Father as revealed in the Son.
keyPoints: The doctrine is ultimately practical, with radical consequences for Christian experience and life
The Trinity and relationships: God lives as the mystery of love among persons
It is the framework for reflecting on the human person and our relation to God and to other creatures
Baptism into the name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit – names express personal identity
God relates to us personally as loving Father, self-giving Saviour and sanctifying Spirit
The Triune God is love; without the Trinity there can be no fellowship as love in God
The communal nature of God obliges us to promote fellowship, solidarity, freedom, justice and peace
The Trinity and prayer – the distinct role of Father, Son and Holy Spirit in Christian prayer

subject: DOC
chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
topic: The Work of the Holy Spirit
question: Identify five (5) of the fruit of the Spirit and explain each one of them.
idealAnswer: In Galatians chapter 5 Paul states the principle of fruit bearing: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such, there is no law” (Gal. 5:22-23). Notice that it is singular – there are not nine fruits but one fruit composed of nine elements, and the one kind of fruit the Spirit produces is Christ-likeness. Love is what God is and what we ought to be; Christ said that his new commandment was that believers should love one another. Joy is contentment and satisfaction with God and with his dealings, a New Testament joy totally independent of circumstances, so that joy and persecution go hand in hand in numerous instances. Peace includes the peace of God as well as harmonious relations among Christians and with others; it is tranquillity of soul, the peace which passes all understanding that Jesus called “my” peace, and it does not mean the absence of trouble but the deep peace that protects. Longsuffering means patience in affliction, annoyance and persecution – patient endurance and steadfastness, whose supreme example is found in Luke 23:34. Kindness is gentleness, best explained in the attitude of the Lord himself. Goodness is kindness shown to others, being kind but firm and ready to do good; it was the transparent goodness of Jesus that drew people to him. Faith here means fidelity or faithfulness, which makes one true to one’s promise and faithful to one’s task. Gentleness is taking the lowly place as Jesus did when he washed his disciples’ feet; it does not mean mildness or weakness but controlled strength. Self-control is the rational restraint of the natural impulses. The fruit is not produced by human effort but as Christians live in communion with the Lord, and it is the evidence of salvation and of the genuine work of the Holy Spirit.
keyPoints: The fruit of the Spirit is one fruit of nine elements (Gal. 5:22-23), producing Christ-likeness
Love – what God is and what we ought to be; Christ’s new commandment
Joy – contentment and satisfaction with God, independent of circumstances
Peace – the peace of God, tranquillity of soul, harmonious relations
Longsuffering – patience in affliction, annoyance and persecution
Kindness and goodness – gentleness, and kindness shown to others, ready to do good
Faith – fidelity, faithfulness to one’s promise and task; gentleness – controlled strength, taking the lowly place
Self-control – rational restraint of the natural impulses; the fruit takes time to mature and is not produced by human effort

subject: DOC
question: Write short notes on any five (5) facts about the Resurrection of Jesus Christ that Christians need to know.
idealAnswer: The resurrection is the central doctrine of Christianity, affirming that God raised Jesus from the dead on the third day; without it, Paul declared, Christian preaching and belief are meaningless, there would be no church and we would still be in our sins. Five things Christians need to know about it are these. First, it is the foundation of the Christian faith: it lifts Christianity from the level of philosophy or a mere code of conduct to the stature of God’s good news for the human race, for in the resurrection God set his seal of approval upon Christ as Son of God and underlined the value of his death; it transformed the followers of Jesus and sent them out to preach, and it is the non-negotiable pivot of the faith. Second, it is an event supported by evidence: there is factual evidence – the empty tomb with only the abandoned grave clothes, the failure of every other explanation, and the numerous reported appearances of the risen Jesus at different times and before different people – and psychological evidence – the transformed disciples, the conviction of the early church under persecution, and the change of the day of worship from Saturday to Sunday. Third, it is a promise of ultimate victory: had Christ not been raised, his death would have been evidence enough of the failure of his mission, but the resurrection assures the believer that he has not believed in vain and that all things, even the last enemy, death, must submit to the victory and rule of Jesus. Fourth, it is the power of Christian experience: the resurrection is far more than a past event, for it plays a vital part in Christian living now and colours the outlook, hopes and motives of every believer, who lives and works in the very power by which God raised Jesus from the dead. Fifth, it is the assurance of eternal security: the finality has been taken out of death, for all who die know that Christ has been through the experience before them and will bring them through it to be with him, and because Christ’s body was raised the Christian is guaranteed a resurrection body of beauty and strength, related to the old but without weakness or decay.
keyPoints: It is the foundation of the Christian faith – the non-negotiable pivot
God set his seal of approval upon Christ as Son of God
It is an event supported by evidence – empty tomb, grave clothes, appearances
Psychological evidence – transformed disciples, the persecuted church, Saturday changed to Sunday
It is a promise of ultimate victory – death, the last enemy, must submit to Jesus
It is the power of Christian experience
It is the assurance of eternal security
The Christian is guaranteed a resurrection body without weakness or decay

subject: DOC
question: State five (5) of the Christological titles of Jesus Christ and elaborate on any three (3) of them.
idealAnswer: The many different names of Jesus Christ reveal the distinctive characteristics of his person and the work that he came to do. Five of his titles are Messiah, the Holy One of God, Son of God, Son of Man, Word and Wisdom, High Priest, Lord, and God. Messiah: for hundreds of years the Jews had been looking for a future King who would be a descendant of David; this person they called the Messiah, which in Greek is Christos, from which we get Christ, and both words mean “the anointed one”. It was Simon Peter who made the first clear declaration that Jesus was the Christ, though Jesus rejected the popular idea of the Messiah as a political deliverer from Rome and saw his messianic role as one of suffering and death for the salvation of humankind. Son of Man: the expression, ben adam in Hebrew and bar nasha in Aramaic, was commonly a periphrasis for “man”. Jesus used this title of himself more than any other, and although it seems to speak of his humanity it is in reality a pointer to his deity; it usually emphasizes his messianic role, for in the Old Testament the Messiah was called the Son of Man in Daniel 7:13-14. He used it in three ways – of his earthly ministry, of his death and of his coming glory. Lord: several words denoting lordship were used of Jesus in the New Testament, and this title is somewhat different from the others, because while the others are descriptive terms “Lord” expresses rank or worth. To acknowledge Jesus Christ as Lord appears to have been one of the earliest Christian confessions of faith, and “Jesus is Lord” is the ultimate Christian creed: when we call Jesus Lord we say something about him and also express our devotion and allegiance, recognizing him as an exalted being. Other titles are the Holy One of God, given to Jesus by Peter as a name belonging to him as the Messiah, especially set apart for God; Son of God, which occurs most frequently in John’s Gospel and usually emphasizes Jesus’ deity; Word and Wisdom, for Jesus is the Logos, the perfect expression of God to humankind and the one through whom all things were created; High Priest, a title given to Christ in the Book of Hebrews and drawn from the Old Testament system of sacrifices; and God, for Thomas confessed the risen Christ as “My Lord and my God”.
keyPoints: The many names of Jesus reveal the distinctive characteristics of his person and work
Messiah / Christ – “the anointed one”; Peter’s first clear declaration
The Holy One of God – given by Peter, a name belonging to him as Messiah
Son of God – most frequent in John; emphasizes Jesus’ deity
Son of Man – Jesus’ favourite self-designation; points to his deity and messianic role (Dan. 7:13-14)
Word and Wisdom – the Logos, the perfect expression of God to humankind
High Priest – given in the Book of Hebrews, drawn from the Old Testament sacrifices
Lord – expresses rank or worth; “Jesus is Lord” is the ultimate Christian creed; and God

subject: DOC
topic: The Biblical Source of the Doctrine of the Trinity
question: The Bible does not teach the doctrine of the Trinity, neither is the word “Trinity” itself found in the Bible. Yet we can find its roots in the Bible. Discuss.
idealAnswer: The Bible does not teach the doctrine of the Trinity: neither the word “trinity” itself nor such language as “one-in-three”, “three-in-one”, one “essence” or “substance”, or three “persons” is biblical language. While we cannot find the doctrine itself spelled out in Scripture, we can find there the roots of the doctrine. In the Old Testament the first root is creation, where Elohim is seen to create by means of Word and Spirit (Gen. 1:1-3), revealing a threefold centre of activity in which God the creator thought out the universe, expressed his thought in a Word and made his Spirit its animating principle; and the name Elohim in Genesis 1:1 is plural in form but joined to a singular verb. A second root is the creation of man and the use of personal pronouns in the plural form, for in Genesis 1:26 God says, “Let us make man in our image and after our likeness,” which by implication reveals God as the Triune God. A third is the threefold Aaronic blessing of Numbers 6:24, a prototype of the New Testament apostolic blessing. In the New Testament, Robert Culver notes two traditional expressions for the inner relations of the persons – the eternal generation of the Son by the Father and the eternal aspiration or procession of the Spirit from the Father and the Son – expressed in John 1:14, which calls our Lord the only begotten Son of the Father, and John 14:16, 26, which speak of the Spirit as proceeding from the Father. The preaching of John the Baptist most probably had a Trinitarian reference. At the baptism of Jesus in the Jordan the three persons can be distinguished: the Son being baptized, the Father speaking from heaven and the Spirit descending in the objective symbol of a dove. In his public ministry and in his private teaching of the Twelve, Jesus constantly directed attention to the Father as the one who sent him and from whom he derived his authority, and bore clear testimony to the Father and the Spirit in the work of redemption. The most concise expression of Trinitarian teaching by Christ is the baptismal formula of Matthew 28:19. Peter explains the Pentecost experience as the activity of the Triune God, and the apostolic benediction shows that the apostolic church was built upon faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. From both Testaments we see the Trinity acting in unity in creation, incarnation, redemption, salvation, communion, prayer, glory and regeneration.

The doctrine is not spelt out in Scripture, but its roots are there

Pentecost, the apostolic benediction, and the Trinity acting in unity in creation, incarnation, redemption and salvation

chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE LAST THINGS (ESCHATOLOGY)
question: Write short notes on any two (2) of the following: (a) Christ’s return (b) Resurrection of the Body (c) The Day of Judgment.
idealAnswer: Christians are not in full agreement about the details of future events, but most writers focus on the return of Christ, the resurrection of the body and the final judgment as the essential and dominant elements of eschatology. Christ’s return occupies a prominent place in the Old Testament, most of whose prophecies about the coming of Christ deal not with his first advent, in which he died as our sin-bearer, but with his Second Advent, in which he is to rule as king. In the New Testament one verse in twenty-five deals with the Lord’s return; it is mentioned 318 times in the 260 chapters and appears in every New Testament book except Galatians and the very short books. Jesus spoke of his return often, Paul’s letters are full of it and he called it “our blessed hope”, while Peter called it our “living hope”. It is a practical doctrine and not an escape route for wishful thoughts: the early Christians associated it with a period of great wickedness on earth, the resurrection and transformation of their bodies, an earthly rule of the glorified Jesus and a final judgment; they acknowledged that their lives should be lived differently because of it; it comforts the suffering and the bereaved, and it is an encouragement to godly living. The resurrection of the body – specifically the resurrection of the bodies of believers at Christ’s Second Coming – is the second point on which Christians are widely agreed. It recognizes that death is an enemy, something unnatural and evil that was not God’s original intention, against the false optimism that denies the reality of sin, suffering and death; and it speaks of the victory over death provided by the Lord Jesus. Death involves every part of our being, for Adam and Eve died in spirit, soul and body; and when God saves us he saves us in spirit, soul and body – a new spirit at the new birth, a new soul through sanctification, a new body at the resurrection – so that his salvation is a complete salvation, assured to us by Christ’s own resurrection. The Day of Judgement will be a joy for Christians, who will be raised to meet Christ, but it will also mean the beginning of Christ’s judgments for those who have contemptuously rejected the gospel, for he will come “to judge the living and the dead”, as Christians acknowledge whenever they recite the Apostles’ Creed. It tells us that history has an end and that its end involves accountability: we shall answer for what we have done and be judged either on the basis of our own righteousness, which will condemn us, or on the basis of the perfect righteousness of Jesus our Saviour. Jesus taught what the final judgment would be like in three parables – the Ten Virgins, the Talents, and the Sheep and Goats – each of which contains the same essential features: a sudden return of the Lord, some prepared for his coming and others not, rewards and judgments, and the amazement of the lost at the outcome.
keyPoints: The dominant elements of eschatology are Christ’s return, the resurrection of the body and the day of judgement
Christ’s return is mentioned in every New Testament book except Galatians and the very short books
Paul: “our blessed hope”; Peter: our “living hope”
The return is a practical doctrine – it shapes conduct, comforts, and encourages godly living
The resurrection of the body recognizes death as an enemy and proclaims victory over it
God saves us in spirit, soul and body – a complete salvation assured by Christ’s resurrection

chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
topic: The Work of the Holy Spirit
question: Discuss the importance of the Holy Spirit to the Christian life.
idealAnswer: The Holy Spirit is mainly featured in the Bible for his work in the lives of men and women. In his general activity he convinces of sin, for as Spirit of truth his work is to convince the unbeliever of being wrong, something achieved not by human means but as he makes the message of the Bible plain; he illuminates truth, for as he inspired the writing of God’s word so he shows us what the Bible means, and without his enlightening work the truth of God’s message remains misty and can even seem nonsensical and offensive; he reveals Christ, for his task is to focus the spotlight not on himself but on Christ, so that in having the Holy Spirit we have Christ; he lives in believers, making Christ real to the Christian, for no one who belongs to Christ is without him; he inspires prayer, helping us because he understands our weaknesses and preventing prayer from degenerating into mechanical drudgery; and he prepares us for heaven, for the whole Christian life is a life directed by the Spirit, who helps the Christian in the battle with sin and prepares him or her for glory. From the beginning of Christian discipleship the Holy Spirit lives within the Christian, giving the power to follow Christ, confidence in believing, and unity with other believers. He gives life – the new birth, for without the power of God a person is spiritually dead, and this new birth is brought about by the Spirit in one who responds to the good news of Christ. He gives assurance – the witness of the Spirit – confirming the reality of the new relationship with Christ, that the believer is a child of God, and that the Bible’s promise of eternal life is to be believed. He gives unity – fellowship in the Spirit, since every Christian has received him. He gives ownership – the seal of the Spirit, the invisible yet permanent stamp of God’s ownership, so that we belong to God and cannot be separated from his love. He gives power – the fullness of the Spirit, which Christians are commanded to know as a continuous and regular experience. And he gives confidence – the pledge of the Spirit, a foretaste of all that God has prepared for his people in the future. He also produces in the believer the fruit of the Spirit, which is Christ-likeness, and distributes gifts for the building up and the mission of the Church.

topic: Hallmark of the Gifts of the Spirit
question: What is (are) the difference(s) between the Fruit of the Holy Spirit and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit?
idealAnswer: The fruit of the Spirit and the gifts of the Spirit are both the work of the one Holy Spirit, but they differ. The fruit of the Spirit is concerned with character, while the gifts of the Spirit relate to abilities and functions distributed among believers. All the fruit should be exhibited in every Christian, but the gifts differ widely from person to person. The fruit is singular, not plural: Paul writes in Galatians 5:22-23 that “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control,” so there are not nine fruits but one fruit composed of nine elements, and the one kind of fruit the Spirit produces is Christ-likeness. Unlike the gifts, only some of which are given to a Christian, each believer is to have all nine virtues composing the fruit; and as fruit on a tree takes time to grow and mature, so the Spirit does not cultivate these virtues in a believer’s life overnight. The fruit is not produced by human effort but as Christians live in communion with the Lord, and it is the evidence of salvation and of the genuine work of the Spirit. The gifts, by contrast, began to be given when the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples at Pentecost and will continue until Christ comes again. They are not restricted to outstanding individuals or leaders: each believer has at least one gift, no one believer possesses all the gifts, and so the members of the Church need one another. Their hallmarks are that they glorify Christ, they involve all, they should unite all, they lay foundations, they edify the Church and they promote its mission; and they can be abused – by not using them in love, by neglecting the gifts imparted to us, or by attempting to use gifts not imparted to us.

topic: The Relevance of the Doctrine of the Trinity
question: Explain the relevance of the Trinity to the Christian life and experience.
idealAnswer: The doctrine of the Trinity is ultimately a practical doctrine with radical consequences for Christian experience and life. First, it shapes relationships. According to the doctrine, God lives as the mystery of love among persons; since we are created in the image and likeness of this God and our destiny is to live for ever with him and with his beloved creatures, the doctrine is a way of contemplating the mystery of God and of ourselves in relation to God, and the framework for reflecting on the nature of the human person and on the relationship between humankind and the other creatures of the earth. Christians are normally baptized into the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and since names express personal identity, to live in the name of another is to appropriate their personal history. Secondly, it shapes our relationship with others. The Godhead reveals that God is truly a living one, not impersonal but personal, who relates and deals with us at one and the same time as loving Father, self-giving Saviour and sanctifying Spirit. The Triune God is Love and is always in love: St. Augustine said that without the Trinity there can be no fellowship as love in God. The Trinity teaches that God is indivisibly one, with unity of purpose and action, the three persons living and working harmoniously together for the promotion and final realization of the Kingdom of God, so that as we worship the God of unity we too are called to unity. It also brings to the fore the communal nature of God: the three persons live in a state of mutual co-existence, solidarity, fellowship and harmony, with no power struggle or personality conflict within the Godhead, and those who embrace this fact are under a moral and spiritual obligation to promote fellowship, solidarity and harmonious communal existence, and through this freedom, justice, peace and prosperity. Thirdly, the doctrine shapes prayer. St. Augustine acknowledged the active presence and involvement of the Triune God in the prayer of Christians, with each Person playing his distinct role: we pray to the Father with the assurance that it is God himself who has given us the power of becoming children of God; prayers are addressed to Christ, as well as through him and in his name, for Jesus taught his disciples to pray and set the example by praying himself; and in prayer the Holy Spirit is the Christian’s master who animates the prayer and enables us to discover God as our Father as revealed in the Son.

topic: The Apostle's Creed and its Explanation
question: What does it mean to say that the church is holy and therefore different from other institutions?
idealAnswer: The basic meaning of the word holy is “different” or “separate”. Since the Church is the body of Christ, and Christ is pure and blameless and was set apart for a purpose, so is the Church. When we confess that the church is holy we do not mean that its members know better or are morally superior to other people; the church is holy because its members are called by God to live unselfish, pure and consecrated lives. There are three ways in which we can say that the church is holy, or different and distinguished from other organizations or groups of people. First, it is a community of people who know they are sinners and freely admit that they are not good or superior. From the time of the prophets to the apostles, individual and social sinfulness have been identified among the people of God and addressed. As Charles C. Morrison aptly put it, the church is not a society of good people; it is a society of sinners, the only organization in human society that takes sinners into its membership just because they are sinners, and the only one that keeps on saying, week after week and age after age, “We have left undone those things which we ought to have done, and we have done those things which we ought not to have done.” Secondly, it is a community of people who are not satisfied with themselves or with the way things are in the world around them: they gather not to justify their present way of life or to publicize their holiness, but to admit publicly that they need to be forgiven for what they are, that they want to change and that they need help. Thirdly, it is a community which is gathered in the name of Jesus Christ, who is its Head. As Guthrie says, holiness is not found in the church and its members as such, but in him from whom they seek forgiveness, change, help and new direction; the church which is the body is holy only because the Head is the “Holy One”.

subject: DOC
question: The Christian faith affirms that Jesus Christ is truly human and truly divine. Discuss five (5) proofs that Jesus was indeed divine and human.
idealAnswer: The story of the birth of Jesus is not just a beautiful idea or an abstract theological truth; it is historical, and the syllabus sets out several facts about the Incarnation which show that Jesus is truly God and truly man. First, Christ was Son of God from eternity: the New Testament teaches that Jesus existed long before he was born and did not come into being at the time of his birth, but has always existed as the Son of God; it was through him that God created the universe, and in him all things hold together. Secondly, it was by supernatural conception: the circumstances of Christ’s birth help us to understand that he was born without sin, for the human inclination to sin is inherited from our parents, and though his birth was as normal as any human’s, his conception occurred through the intervention of the Holy Spirit, so that Jesus was both God and man. Thirdly, it upholds Christ’s full deity: as the New Testament unfolds, the fact that Christ is God is increasingly revealed in his character, for he lived his life without a taint of sin; in his claims, to be the centre of all truth, the world’s judge and to have a unique relationship to the Father; and in his conduct, in performing miracles, forgiving sins and accepting worship. Fourthly, it establishes Christ’s full humanity: the New Testament shows that Christ was fully human, born into a Hebrew family and subject to the Hebrew law, experiencing all the problems people face – hunger and thirst, fatigue and sorrow – and facing the full force of temptation; although still fully God, he shared completely the weaknesses of all humankind except sin, and so was perfectly qualified to be the unique go-between bringing humankind and God together. Fifthly, it explains Christ’s unique personality: he is both God and man, in two distinct natures and one person for ever – the same Jesus who declared that he was thirsty also referred in prayer to the glory which he shared eternally with the Father. Sixthly, it validates Christ’s saving ministry: we know enough to realize that Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, is the one Saviour humankind needs, for by laying aside his eternal splendour and involving himself in humankind’s burdens, even to death on the cross, he becomes the reconciler between God and humankind. The Bible thus presents Christ as altogether God and altogether man – the perfect mediator between God and humankind because he partakes fully of the nature of both.
keyPoints: Christ was Son of God from eternity – he did not come into being at his birth
It was by supernatural conception – through the intervention of the Holy Spirit, so he was both God and man
It upholds Christ’s full deity – his character, his claims and his conduct
It establishes Christ’s full humanity – hunger, thirst, fatigue, sorrow and temptation
It explains Christ’s unique personality – two distinct natures, one person for ever
It validates Christ’s saving ministry – truly God and truly man, the one Saviour we need
He shared the weaknesses of humankind except sin, and so is the unique go-between
The Bible presents Christ as altogether God and altogether man

subject: DOC
question: Write short notes on five facts about the Resurrection of Jesus Christ that Christians need to bear in mind.
idealAnswer: The resurrection is the central doctrine of Christianity, affirming that God raised Jesus from the dead on the third day; without it, Paul declared, Christian preaching and belief are meaningless, there would be no church and we would still be in our sins. Five things Christians need to know about it are these. First, it is the foundation of the Christian faith: it lifts Christianity from the level of philosophy or a mere code of conduct to the stature of God’s good news for the human race, for in the resurrection God set his seal of approval upon Christ as Son of God and underlined the value of his death; it transformed the followers of Jesus and sent them out to preach, and it is the non-negotiable pivot of the faith. Second, it is an event supported by evidence: there is factual evidence – the empty tomb with only the abandoned grave clothes, the failure of every other explanation, and the numerous reported appearances of the risen Jesus at different times and before different people – and psychological evidence – the transformed disciples, the conviction of the early church under persecution, and the change of the day of worship from Saturday to Sunday. Third, it is a promise of ultimate victory: had Christ not been raised, his death would have been evidence enough of the failure of his mission, but the resurrection assures the believer that he has not believed in vain and that all things, even the last enemy, death, must submit to the victory and rule of Jesus. Fourth, it is the power of Christian experience: the resurrection is far more than a past event, for it plays a vital part in Christian living now and colours the outlook, hopes and motives of every believer, who lives and works in the very power by which God raised Jesus from the dead. Fifth, it is the assurance of eternal security: the finality has been taken out of death, for all who die know that Christ has been through the experience before them and will bring them through it to be with him, and because Christ’s body was raised the Christian is guaranteed a resurrection body of beauty and strength, related to the old but without weakness or decay.

God set his seal of approval upon Christ as Son of God
It is an event supported by evidence – empty tomb, grave clothes, appearances
Psychological evidence – transformed disciples, the persecuted church, Saturday changed to Sunday
It is a promise of ultimate victory – death, the last enemy, must submit to Jesus
It is the power of Christian experience
It is the assurance of eternal security
The Christian is guaranteed a resurrection body without weakness or decay

subject: DOC
chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
topic: Hallmark of the Gifts of the Spirit
question: What is/are the difference(s) between the Fruit of the Holy Spirit and the Gifts of the Holy Spirit?
idealAnswer: The fruit of the Spirit and the gifts of the Spirit are both the work of the one Holy Spirit, but they differ. The fruit of the Spirit is concerned with character, while the gifts of the Spirit relate to abilities and functions distributed among believers. All the fruit should be exhibited in every Christian, but the gifts differ widely from person to person. The fruit is singular, not plural: Paul writes in Galatians 5:22-23 that “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control,” so there are not nine fruits but one fruit composed of nine elements, and the one kind of fruit the Spirit produces is Christ-likeness. Unlike the gifts, only some of which are given to a Christian, each believer is to have all nine virtues composing the fruit; and as fruit on a tree takes time to grow and mature, so the Spirit does not cultivate these virtues in a believer’s life overnight. The fruit is not produced by human effort but as Christians live in communion with the Lord, and it is the evidence of salvation and of the genuine work of the Spirit. The gifts, by contrast, began to be given when the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples at Pentecost and will continue until Christ comes again. They are not restricted to outstanding individuals or leaders: each believer has at least one gift, no one believer possesses all the gifts, and so the members of the Church need one another. Their hallmarks are that they glorify Christ, they involve all, they should unite all, they lay foundations, they edify the Church and they promote its mission; and they can be abused – by not using them in love, by neglecting the gifts imparted to us, or by attempting to use gifts not imparted to us.

subject: DOC
topic: The Apostle's Creed and its Explanation
question: How would you explain the fact that the church is holy and therefore different from other organizations or groups of people?
idealAnswer: The basic meaning of the word holy is “different” or “separate”. Since the Church is the body of Christ, and Christ is pure and blameless and was set apart for a purpose, so is the Church. When we confess that the church is holy we do not mean that its members know better or are morally superior to other people; the church is holy because its members are called by God to live unselfish, pure and consecrated lives. There are three ways in which we can say that the church is holy, or different and distinguished from other organizations or groups of people. First, it is a community of people who know they are sinners and freely admit that they are not good or superior. From the time of the prophets to the apostles, individual and social sinfulness have been identified among the people of God and addressed. As Charles C. Morrison aptly put it, the church is not a society of good people; it is a society of sinners, the only organization in human society that takes sinners into its membership just because they are sinners, and the only one that keeps on saying, week after week and age after age, “We have left undone those things which we ought to have done, and we have done those things which we ought not to have done.” Secondly, it is a community of people who are not satisfied with themselves or with the way things are in the world around them: they gather not to justify their present way of life or to publicize their holiness, but to admit publicly that they need to be forgiven for what they are, that they want to change and that they need help. Thirdly, it is a community which is gathered in the name of Jesus Christ, who is its Head. As Guthrie says, holiness is not found in the church and its members as such, but in him from whom they seek forgiveness, change, help and new direction; the church which is the body is holy only because the Head is the “Holy One”.

The Church is the body of Christ, who is pure and blameless and set apart
Holiness does not mean the members are morally superior

It is a community of people who know they are sinners – Morrison: a society of sinners
It is a community not satisfied with itself or the world, gathered to admit its need of forgiveness and change
It is a community gathered in the name of Jesus Christ, its Head
Guthrie: holiness is found in him from whom they seek forgiveness and new direction

subject: DOC
question: Write short notes on the following Christological titles: (a) Messiah (b) God (c) Lord (d) Son of Man.
idealAnswer: The many different names of Jesus Christ reveal the distinctive characteristics of his person and the work that he came to do. Messiah: for hundreds of years the Jews had been looking for a future King who would be a descendant of David when Jesus came into the world; this person they called the Messiah, which in Greek is Christos, from which we get Christ, and both words mean “the anointed one” or “one who has been anointed”. He would have God’s authority and power to bring in the end of the age and establish the kingdom of God. It was Simon Peter who made the first clear declaration that Jesus was the Christ, but Jesus totally rejected the popular idea of the Messiah as a political deliverer from the Roman Empire and saw his messianic role as one of suffering and death for the salvation of humankind; the Jews, looking for a king who would lead their nation to political victory over Rome, did not believe the Messiah would be God himself come to earth as a man or that he would die on a cross. God: Jesus is called God in the New Testament. Thomas, convinced that the risen Christ stood before him, abandoned his doubts with the confession, “My Lord and my God!”, and the classic text is John 1:1, where John declared that the Word existed not only “in the beginning”, where he was “with God”, but also actually “was God”. Lord: several words denoting lordship were used of Jesus in the New Testament. This title is somewhat different from the other titles, because whilst the others are descriptive terms, “Lord” expresses rank or worth. To acknowledge Jesus Christ as Lord appears to have been one of the earliest Christian confessions of faith, and “Jesus is Lord” is the ultimate Christian creed; when we call Jesus “Lord” we are certainly saying something about him as well as expressing our devotion and allegiance to him, recognizing him as an exalted being. As Graham Stanton puts it, the kyrios Christology expresses the authority of the Lord over the individual and the Christian community, and is often related to ethical statements. Son of Man: the expression, ben adam in Hebrew and bar nasha in Aramaic, was commonly used as a periphrasis for “man”. Jesus used this title more than any other to describe himself; although it seems to speak of his humanity, in reality it is a pointer to his deity, and it usually emphasizes his messianic role, for in the Old Testament the Messiah was called the Son of Man in Daniel 7:13-14. He used the title in three ways: when speaking of his earthly ministry, of his death and of his coming glory. The terms “Son of God” and “Son of Man” are used interchangeably in Matthew 26:63-65.
keyPoints: The many names of Jesus reveal the characteristics of his person and work
Messiah/Christ means “the anointed one”; Peter made the first clear declaration
Jesus rejected the political idea of the Messiah and saw his role as suffering and death
God – Thomas’s confession “My Lord and my God”; the classic text John 1:1
Lord – expresses rank or worth, unlike the descriptive titles
“Jesus is Lord” is the ultimate Christian creed and an early confession of faith
Son of Man – ben adam / bar nasha; Jesus’ favourite self-designation
Son of Man points to his deity and his messianic role (Dan. 7:13-14), used of his ministry, death and coming glory

subject: DOC
topic: The Work of Jesus can be discussed in terms of past, present, and future:
question: Discuss the work of Christ in terms of past, present and future.
idealAnswer: The work of Jesus can be discussed in terms of past, present and future. By the “finished” work of Christ is meant the work of atonement or redemption for the human race which he completed by his death on the Cross. This work is so perfect in itself that it requires neither repetition nor addition, and because of it he is called “Saviour of the world”. His finished work broke hell’s powers: Colossians 2:15 speaks of the “principalities and powers” as the evil powers which have controlled humanity, against which there was no hope of successful resistance, and when it looked as if death and hell had conquered him too, he conquered them on the cross. The saving work of Christ therefore includes the reconciliation of sinners to God and also brings them together as human beings, so that hostile divisions of humanity have peace with one another through him. The present work of Christ begins with his exaltation by God, after the completion of his finished work in his death and resurrection. Its first aspect was the sending of the Holy Spirit to dwell in his people, the fulfilment of which Peter announced. The aspect of his present work which receives the main emphasis in the New Testament is his intercession: Jesus’ presence with God as his people’s representative provides the assurance that their requests for spiritual help are heard and granted, and to know that he is there is a powerful incentive to his followers, since no good thing that Jesus seeks for them is withheld by the Father. His exaltation is repeatedly presented in the New Testament as the fulfilment of Psalm 110:1, “Sit at My right hand, till I make your enemies your footstool,” which means that Christ reigns from his present place of exaltation and must do so until all his enemies are overthrown. The future work of Christ is the raising of the dead and the passing of final judgment. To raise the dead and to judge the world are prerogatives of God, but he delegated these works to his Son to discharge at the time of the end, and they are associated with the Second Coming of Christ; Paul viewed Christ’s appearing in glory as the occasion when his people would share his glory and be displayed to the universe as the sons and daughters of God. Both the present work of Christ and his future work depend upon his finished work, which was the beginning of God’s good work in his people – a work that will not be completed until “the day of Jesus Christ”, when the entire universe will be united in Christ.

subject: DOC
chapter: THE DOCTRINE OF THE HOLY SPIRIT
topic: The Work of the Holy Spirit
question: Write a sermon to your congregation explaining how the Holy Spirit works in the life of a Christian.
idealAnswer: The Holy Spirit is mainly featured in the Bible for his work in the lives of men and women. In his general activity he convinces of sin, for as Spirit of truth his work is to convince the unbeliever of being wrong – something achieved not by human means but as he makes the message of the Bible plain; he illuminates truth, for as he inspired the writing of God’s word so he shows us what it means, and without his enlightening work the truth of God’s message remains misty and can even seem nonsensical and offensive; he reveals Christ, for his task is to focus the spotlight not on himself but on Christ, so that in having the Holy Spirit we have Christ; he lives in believers, making Christ real to the Christian, for no one who belongs to Christ is without him; he inspires prayer, helping us because he understands our weaknesses and preventing prayer from degenerating into mechanical drudgery or powerless routine; and he prepares us for heaven, for the whole Christian life is a life directed by the Spirit, who helps the Christian in the battle with sin and prepares him or her for glory. From the beginning of Christian discipleship the Holy Spirit lives within the Christian, giving the power to follow Christ, confidence in believing, and unity with other believers. He gives life – the new birth, for without the power of God a person is spiritually dead, and this new birth is brought about by the Spirit in one who responds to the good news of Christ, and is not earned by personal achievement but is God’s free gift. He gives assurance – the witness of the Spirit – confirming the reality of the believer’s new relationship with Christ, that he or she is a child of God, and that the Bible’s promise of eternal life is to be believed. He gives unity – fellowship in the Spirit. He gives ownership – the seal of the Spirit, the invisible yet permanent stamp of God’s ownership, so that we belong to God and cannot be separated from his love. He gives power – the fullness of the Spirit, which Christians are commanded to know as a continuous and regular experience. And he gives confidence – the pledge of the Spirit, a foretaste of all that God has prepared for his people. He also produces in the believer the fruit of the Spirit, which is Christ-likeness, and distributes gifts for the building up and mission of the Church.

He lives in believers and inspires prayer
He prepares the Christian for heaven

Assurance – the witness of the Spirit; unity – fellowship in the Spirit

subject: DOC
topic: The Apostle's Creed and its Explanation
question: How will you explain to a non-Christian friend the fact that the church is holy and therefore different from other organizations or groups of people?
idealAnswer: The basic meaning of the word holy is “different” or “separate”. Since the Church is the body of Christ, and Christ is pure and blameless and was set apart for a purpose, so is the Church. When we confess that the church is holy we do not mean that its members know better or are morally superior to other people; the church is holy because its members are called by God to live unselfish, pure and consecrated lives. There are three ways in which we can say that the church is holy, or different and distinguished from other organizations or groups of people. First, it is a community of people who know they are sinners and freely admit that they are not good or superior. From the time of the prophets to the apostles, individual and social sinfulness have been identified among the people of God and addressed. As Charles C. Morrison aptly put it, the church is not a society of good people; it is a society of sinners, the only organization in human society that takes sinners into its membership just because they are sinners, and the only one that keeps on saying, week after week and age after age, “We have left undone those things which we ought to have done, and we have done those things which we ought not to have done.” Secondly, it is a community of people who are not satisfied with themselves or with the way things are in the world around them: they gather not to justify their present way of life or to publicize their holiness, but to admit publicly that they need to be forgiven for what they are, that they want to change and that they need help. Thirdly, it is a community which is gathered in the name of Jesus Christ, who is its Head. As Guthrie says, holiness is not found in the church and its members as such, but in him from whom they seek forgiveness, change, help and new direction; the church which is the body is holy only because the Head is the “Holy One”.
keyPoints: The basic meaning of holy is “different” or “separate”
The Church is the body of Christ, who is pure and blameless and set apart
Holiness does not mean the members are morally superior
Its members are called by God to live unselfish, pure and consecrated lives
